headline: Pelicans fans are a small, fiercely local, Saints-first and Mardi Gras-literate base who love the city's culture louder than the team's results, and are tired of waiting for a Zion-led payoff.
summary: New Orleans is a Saints, LSU and Mardi Gras town first, and the Pelicans hold a loyal but modest slice of it, strongest among diehards who stayed through the Hornets-to-Pelicans transition and the Anthony Davis years. Two straight sub-30-win seasons (26-56 last year), a quiet offseason under Joe Dumars, and a new coach in Jamahl Mosley have left the mood weary and wait-and-see rather than angry. Zion Williamson is still the emotional lightning rod, Trey Murphy III is the player fans actually trust, and second-year players Derik Queen and Jeremiah Fears supply the hope. The fan wears the city, not just the team: fleur-de-lis, Mardi Gras purple-green-gold, and local brands sit beside navy and gold Pelicans gear, and the best City Edition moments have come when the team leaned into that.

insights.title: Saints-first town, Pels as the second love
insights.detail: Football, LSU and Carnival dominate the calendar and the closet in New Orleans, so Pelicans gear competes with black-and-gold Saints and purple-and-gold LSU apparel for the same wardrobe slot. Pelicans passion is real but concentrated, and it peaks when the team tells a New Orleans story instead of a generic NBA one.
insights.implication: Lead Pelicans product with city iconography (fleur-de-lis, Carnival, second-line) rather than team marks alone, and avoid directly mimicking Saints black and gold.

insights.title: Fatigue, not fury, is the mood
insights.detail: Last season finished 26-56 and missed the playoffs for the second straight sub-30-win year. Fans are watching a coach change from Willie Green to Jamahl Mosley, no 2026 first-round pick (traded to Atlanta in the Derik Queen deal), and a quiet summer.
insights.implication: Keep early-season product and campaigns about the city and the young core, not championship promises. Trey Murphy III, Queen and Fears are safer faces than anything built on Zion availability.

insights.title: Zion is the brand, Murphy is the trust
insights.detail: Zion Williamson draws national attention and the biggest jersey and sneaker interest, but years of injury interruptions made fans cautious about hanging identity on him. Trey Murphy III, who averaged 21.5 ppg and survived June trade rumors, is the locally admired homegrown-feeling scorer.
insights.implication: Balance Zion signature storytelling with Murphy and young-core product so a single availability story does not govern the line. Zion is already a Jordan Brand athlete, so coordinate any Jordan crossover thinking.

insights.title: Hornets-era memory is the elder's tattoo
insights.detail: Older fans remember the 2002-2013 Hornets era and the Chris Paul, David West, Tyson Chandler and Byron Scott years, plus the 2005-07 Oklahoma City exile after Katrina. Teal and purple Hornets throwbacks still circulate in the city, and the name Pelicans arrived in 2013.
insights.implication: A Hornets-era-adjacent teal and purple heritage gesture could resonate, but the Hornets name and marks belong to Charlotte, so any use needs clear licensing and care.

insights.title: City Edition is the fan's favorite product moment
insights.detail: Per the current facts, the 2025-26 City Edition resurrected the 2023-24 fan-favorite design, which signals that the audience rewards local storytelling and punishes generic. The 2023-24 'NOLA Nights' edition (purple and neon green, a skeletal 'Skelican') shows fans reward a nocturnal, local-feeling look over generic team color.
insights.implication: Treat the City Edition as the anchor drop for the market and pair it with a lifestyle capsule rooted in Carnival color blocking, built with local collaborators.

insights.title: Mardi Gras Indian imagery is not a motif to lift
insights.detail: Black Masking Indian suits and the Tremé and Seventh Ward second-line brass-band culture are sacred community traditions made by the maskers over a full year. Fans love and display the culture but the community is protective of it.
insights.implication: Any reference needs Black New Orleans partners credited and paid, and the suits themselves should not be reproduced as a pattern. Safer cues are the bold, unaffiliated visual languages of Carnival parades, social aid and pleasure club umbrella and sash color play, and brass-band typography.

places.name: Smoothie King Center
places.why: The Pelicans' home next to the Caesars Superdome, where gameday crowds share the footprint with Saints football.

places.name: Caesars Superdome
places.why: The Saints' home is the town's biggest sports cathedral and sets the black-and-gold gameday template Pelicans fans live beside.

places.name: Mother's Restaurant
places.why: A long-standing local institution for ferdi special po-boys and ham, near the arena.

places.name: Frenchmen Street
places.why: The live music corridor where locals gather before and after games and where brass bands and jazz set the soundtrack.

places.name: Congo Square (Armstrong Park)
places.why: The historic gathering place for African and Afro-Creole music and dance and a cultural anchor for any respectful community engagement.

places.name: Bayou St. John
places.why: A Sunday casual hangout area for locals, useful as a lifestyle activation backdrop.

places.name: Tulane University and Loyola area uptown courts
places.why: College basketball presence and rec courts that tie the local hooper community to the city.

people.name: Zion Williamson
people.why: The franchise's most famous player and highest-profile jersey and shoe draw, with a complicated, hopeful relationship with fans.

people.name: Trey Murphy III
people.why: The breakout scorer who averaged 21.5 ppg and whose June trade rumors made fans fiercely protective of him.

people.name: Derik Queen
people.why: Young big acquired in a trade that cost the 2026 first-round pick, now central to the rebuilding hope.

people.name: Jeremiah Fears
people.why: Young guard fans see as a future creator for the team.

people.name: Jamahl Mosley
people.why: First-year coach hired from Orlando in May after Willie Green was dismissed.

people.name: Anthony Davis
people.why: The unibrow-era face of the Pelicans brand who remains the franchise's defining homegrown star in fan memory.

people.name: Chris Paul
people.why: The Hornets-era superstar whose New Orleans years the older fan base remembers most fondly.

people.name: Pete Maravich
people.role: LSU and New Orleans Jazz legend
people.why: Pistol Pete is the Louisiana basketball myth whose floppy-socks era loops into the state's hoops identity.

moments.name: Season opener and NBA Cup run
moments.why: The Pelicans are in West Group B with OKC, MIN, LAC and MEM, with Cup play opening Oct 30 at the Clippers, the first chance to sell local hope.

moments.name: Saints football season overlap
moments.why: The fall and winter football calendar competes for fans' attention and wardrobe, so basketball activation should sit around, not against, Saints Sundays.

moments.name: Christmas and Reveillon season
moments.why: Family gifting peaks, and Pelicans is not on the national Christmas Day slate, so local holiday merchandising matters.

moments.name: Carnival season and Mardi Gras
moments.timing: Twelfth Night (Jan 6) through Fat Tuesday, which falls in February 2027
moments.why: The single biggest color and culture moment of the year, when purple, green and gold override team colors across the city.

moments.name: New Orleans Jazz and Heritage Festival
moments.why: A cultural peak for local pride and fashion, overlapping with the end of the NBA regular season.

moments.name: NBA draft and free agency
moments.why: A hope-and-anxiety moment for a fan base that has watched picks traded and stars leave.

vocabulary.meaning: Common shorthand for the Pelicans among fans and media.
Louisiana's playful spelling of go, as in Geaux Tigers, used in sports chants and gear across the state.
The Saints' signature chant, a reminder of the football-first culture, not a Pelicans phrase.
The brass-band parade tradition whose followers dance behind the main line, used as shorthand for communal celebration.
Local word for a street median, a quick insider tell.
Classic New Orleans greeting and the name of the local accent group.
The Carnival parade call from the crowd to riders on floats.
The French heraldic lily that serves as the city's most recognized emblem and appears on both Saints and Pelicans-adjacent gear.

designCues.cue: Pelicans navy as the base field
designCues.use: Use as the anchor for Association and lifestyle product so team identity stays legible.

designCues.cue: Old-gold accent distinct from Saints metallic
designCues.source: A brass-like accent chosen for this brief; the official Pelicans gold is #85714D
designCues.use: Use as a brass-like accent so it reads as New Orleans, not Saints.

designCues.source: Mardi Gras royal purple, representing justice
designCues.use: Use for colorblocking in Carnival capsule drops, and tie to the season window around Twelfth Night through Fat Tuesday.
Use as a secondary pop on warm-up and lifestyle pieces during Carnival.
Use as a tonal embossed or woven accent, redrawn with distinct proportions so it does not mimic the Saints mark.
Use as a fine tonal jacquard on trims, hems and lining, in a stylized rather than literal rendering.

designCues.cue: Shotgun house and bright-paint color story
designCues.source: Neighborhood architecture of the Seventh Ward, Marigny and Bywater
designCues.use: Use as a color-block palette for a rotating lifestyle capsule, credited to local architectural heritage.

designCues.source: Hand-painted show posters and social aid and pleasure club banners
designCues.use: Use for graphic tees and hoodies, commissioning a local lettering artist.

productHooks: A Carnival-season capsule in purple, green and Pelicans navy and gold, launching in January and ending Fat Tuesday, made with a New Orleans lettering artist or collective.
A tonal fleur-de-lis and iron-lace jacquard warm-up and shooting shirt that ties to the City Edition story.
Murphy, Queen and Fears player-led tees and kids' jerseys so the line is not Zion-dependent.
A Hornets-era heritage nod (teal and purple), only if licensing with the NBA and Charlotte is cleared.
Family-sized and youth Icon and Statement jerseys for the lower-priced entry point, given the base is local and family-heavy.
watchouts: Mardi Gras Indian suits, chants and Black Masking Indian imagery are sacred community traditions. Do not reproduce them as a pattern, and partner with credited, paid community members if referenced at all.
The fleur-de-lis is heavily associated with the Saints, so a derivative mark risks looking like NFL product and may raise third-party licensing issues.
Hornets name, teal and Hugo imagery is controlled by Charlotte and the NBA, so any heritage use requires clearance.
Zion's availability history can make hero-driven campaigns brittle, so avoid a single-athlete dependency.
Avoid caricature in New Orleans iconography, such as jazz-hands, voodoo and excess bourbon-street tropes.

extra.sentiment: Weary and cautious. After a 26-56 season, a coaching change to Jamahl Mosley, no 2026 first-round pick and a quiet offseason under Joe Dumars, fans are lowering expectations, protective of Trey Murphy III, hopeful about Derik Queen and Jeremiah Fears, and still waiting on Zion Williamson.
extra.gamedayLook: A mix of navy and gold Pelicans jerseys (Zion, Murphy, throwback Davis), Hornets-era teal or purple throwbacks on older fans, Saints and LSU gear mixed in, and casual New Orleans summer-weight clothing such as breathable tees, caps and sneakers suited to the heat.
